cues.text: Born around 801 in Picardy , in what is now northern France, Ansgar entered the Benedictine monastery of Corbie as a young man.
He later moved to the daughter house of Corvey in Westphalia, where he taught and preached before being drawn into the great missionary project of his age: bringing Christianity to Scandinavia.
In 826, Ansgar accompanied the newly baptized but soon-exiled Danish King Harald toward his homeland and founded a school at Schleswig.
Within a few years, renewed political turmoil and Harald's second expulsion caused the mission to collapse, forcing Ansgar's return to Frankish territory.
Undeterred, Ansgar set out for Sweden in 829 at the invitation of Emperor Louis the Pious after a Swedish delegation requested Christian missionaries.

His ship was attacked by pirates along the way, but he and his companion Witmar reached Birka regardless and were cordially received by King Björn, winning a number of converts including a royal official named Heriger.
In 831, Louis the Pious made Ansgar the first bishop of a newly created see at Hamburg , with Pope Gregory IV naming him papal legate for the entire Scandinavian mission field.
Disaster struck in 845 when raiding Northmen burned Hamburg to the ground, destroying over a decade of missionary work and driving Scandinavia largely back into paganism.

Rather than abandon the mission, Ansgar secured the union of Hamburg with the vacant see of Bremen, formally ratified by Pope Nicholas I in 864, giving the Northern mission a more secure and permanent base.

He returned personally to Denmark and Sweden in his final years, converting the Danish King Haarik and helping bring about a favorable royal verdict for continued Christian preaching in Sweden as well.

Ansgar died peacefully at Bremen on February 3, 865, having spent nearly four decades laboring, often with heartbreakingly little lasting success in his own lifetime, to plant Christianity in a pagan and unstable North.
Though much of his direct missionary work was undone by pagan reaction after his death, his sustained example laid essential groundwork.

The missionary structures he built at Hamburg-Bremen likewise supported Scandinavia's eventual, permanent Christianization in the centuries that followed, earning him the enduring title Apostle of the North.
